blocks.text: Building on the gaps identified across the three reviewed domains, this section presents the proposed conceptual architecture of SentriZK. It is important to state at the outset that the architecture described here is a design-stage proposal: it consolidates mechanisms that have each been validated independently in the literature into a single unified platform, but the integrated system has not yet been implemented, and no experimental measurements of SentriZK itself are reported in this work. The intent is to articulate a coherent design rationale that draws together established end-to-end encrypted transport [P5], non-interactive zero-knowledge authentication [P6], [P7], [P8], and lightweight on-device threat detection [P2], [P3], [P9], [P10], [P11], [P12], and to make explicit the open challenges that empirical follow-up work must address.

Four design goals direct the proposed architecture. The first is confidentiality: every message must remain unreadable to any intermediary, including the messaging server, which is achieved by retaining well-vetted end-to-end encryption primitives so that only the communicating endpoints can decrypt content [P5]. The second is privacy-preserving authentication: a user must be able to prove possession of a valid credential without transmitting a password, secret, or other disclosable factor, thereby eliminating the disclosure-based risk of conventional login and the human-error-prone manual fingerprint-verification ceremonies that current encrypted messengers rely upon [P1], [P6], [P7]. The third is on-device intelligence: threat detection over both message content and behavioural signals must execute locally so that no raw user data leaves the device, avoiding the cloud latency and privacy leakage inherent in server-side analysis [P3], [P9], [P10], [P11]. The fourth is usability: because prior work shows that optional, manually performed security tasks are routinely skipped or failed by users [P1], trust establishment and threat screening in SentriZK are designed to be automatic and transparent, removing human intervention from the critical security path rather than delegating it to the user.

SentriZK is organised as a layered architecture in which each layer addresses one of the design goals and maps onto a body of validated prior work. Fig. 1 illustrates the layered architecture of SentriZK. The lowest layer is an end-to-end encrypted transport layer that derives an identical shared secret on each client using Diffie-Hellman and Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman key exchange without transmitting private keys, and encrypts messages with AES-256 before transmission, so that messages stored or relayed by the server remain decryptable only by the endpoints holding the shared key [P5]. This layer is hosted on a modular, horizontally scalable backend of the kind demonstrated for E2EE chat, comprising an API gateway, an authentication service, a real-time WebSocket service, a chat service, an encrypted-at-rest datastore, and an asynchronous message broker, which provides scalability and reduces single points of failure [P5].

Above the transport layer sits a zero-knowledge authentication layer that replaces password transmission and manual verification ceremonies with a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof. SentriZK proposes Groth16 zk-SNARKs, in which the prover produces a small proof that is fast to verify but depends on a one-time trusted setup, a trade-off favoured over interactive proofs and over zk-STARKs whose larger proofs impose unattractive bandwidth and storage costs on mobile clients [P6]. This choice is supported by evidence that non-interactive zero-knowledge authentication natively provides anonymity and man-in-the-middle resistance with lower computational and communication overhead than PKI, and can satisfy the energy and computation budgets of constrained devices [P7], and by a deployed zk-SNARK identity-management system of the same Pinocchio/Groth16 family that delivers password-less, identity-hiding authentication on a real cryptographic stack [P8]. The topmost layer is an on-device detection layer running compact models via TensorFlow Lite. It performs two complementary functions: behavioural insider-threat and anomaly detection over sequential signals such as access and activity logs using bidirectional LSTM and related deep sequence models [P2], [P3], [P9], and content-based phishing and smishing detection over message text and embedded links using compressed transformers and lightweight ensembles [P10], [P11], [P12]. Each layer is loosely coupled so that the authentication and detection layers can evolve independently of the transport substrate.

The proposed authentication flow allows a user to prove possession of a valid enterprise credential without ever revealing it. During an enrolment phase, the user's secret is bound to a public commitment, and a one-time trusted setup generates the proving and verification parameters for the authentication circuit, following the parameter-generation model intrinsic to zk-SNARK constructions [P6], [P8]. At login, the client device acts as the prover and generates a non-interactive proof attesting that it knows a secret consistent with the stored commitment; the server acts as the verifier and accepts or rejects the proof without learning the secret, since a zero-knowledge proof convinces the verifier that a statement is true while revealing nothing beyond its validity [P6]. Because the proof is non-interactive, the multi-round challenge-response exchange of interactive protocols is collapsed into a single message, reducing both prover and verifier burden and making the flow suitable for mobile, real-time use [P7]. This design directly targets the residual weakness of encrypted messengers, in which active man-in-the-middle resistance depends on users completing optional, error-prone fingerprint ceremonies [P1]; by authenticating cryptographically rather than through human comparison, SentriZK removes the user from the trust-establishment step. The identity-management work of Luong and Park further illustrates how such a flow can be hardened, for example through a per-proof nonce that prevents certificate reuse and collusion, and how selective disclosure of minor attributes and threshold-based traceability can balance privacy with the accountability an enterprise requires [P8].

The detection pipeline is designed so that inference occurs entirely on the user's device and no raw message content or behavioural data is transmitted off-device for analysis, preserving privacy while avoiding cloud latency [P10], [P11]. Incoming and outgoing messages, once decrypted locally by the legitimate endpoint, are passed through a content-screening stage that applies a compact transformer such as a TinyBERT-based classifier to flag phishing and smishing text, a configuration shown to achieve high accuracy on Android-oriented detection while remaining lightweight [P10], with efficiency-aware model selection guided by composite training, inference, and real-time detection metrics so that latency and battery budgets are respected [P11]. Embedded links are additionally screened by a fast, content-independent URL classifier of the kind that reaches high accuracy with low latency and no third-party dependency [P12]. In parallel, a behavioural stage feeds sequential activity signals into a bidirectional LSTM detector to surface insider-threat and anomaly patterns over time [P2], [P3], [P9]. Models are intended to be converted to TensorFlow Lite for on-device execution; the literature on running LSTM-based anomaly detection on mobile and Android devices confirms the feasibility of this approach while noting its time and bandwidth demands [P9]. Detection outcomes are surfaced as local alerts and never require exporting user data, keeping the second pillar consistent with the platform's privacy-preserving goal.

The proposed architecture can be qualitatively mapped onto the enterprise messaging attack surface enumerated by structured threat modelling [P4]. Spoofing and unauthorised access are countered by the zero-knowledge authentication layer, which establishes identity cryptographically without disclosing credentials and without depending on a fragile manual ceremony [P1], [P6], [P8]. Information disclosure and tampering in transit are addressed by the end-to-end encrypted transport layer, in which only the endpoints can decrypt content even against a compromised server [P5], directly mitigating the incomplete encryption coverage that case studies identify as a recurring weakness [P4]. Insider misuse, which threat modelling flags as a high-priority, human-factor risk, is targeted by the on-device behavioural detection layer that monitors for anomalous activity by otherwise authorised users [P2], [P3], [P4], while phishing, smishing, and impersonation vectors are screened at the content layer [P10], [P11], [P12]. In this way SentriZK consolidates the technical, monitoring, and authentication controls that the threat model recommends, and answers its explicit call to fuse AI-driven anomaly detection with the broader security design [P4]. Several open challenges remain and define the empirical agenda for future work. zk-SNARK proof generation is computationally heavy on mobile hardware: reported figures include large proving keys and multi-second proving times, with infeasibility on devices below modest memory thresholds, underscoring the need for lighter proving and zk-SNARK-friendly circuits and the avoidance of on-chain settlement for routine login [P7], [P8]. On-device detection faces complementary constraints of model size, inference latency, and battery consumption, and the reviewed detection studies notably omit measured on-device latency, memory, and model-size figures, leaving these as the central questions a SentriZK prototype must resolve [P9], [P11]. Because the architecture is a proposal, all such trade-offs are currently grounded in the cited prior work rather than in measurements of the integrated system, and validating them empirically is the immediate next step.
